name: Laurentian
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.note: Extinct 16th-c. Iroquoian attested only via Cartier-era wordlists (cf. Julian 2010 reconstruction); no stress information recoverable.

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.3 languoid page laur1250 and reference records 11407 (Julian 2010) and 703916 (Mithun 2023, 'The value of family relations for revitalization', OUP, pp. 315-336).
sources.note: Only two references listed for the languoid; the Mithun 2023 record is coded for Susquehannock [sqn] (comparative/wordlist/specific feature), not a Laurentian phonology.

sources.citation: Julian, Charles. 2010. A history of the Iroquoian languages. PhD thesis, University of Manitoba. Chapter 9 'Laurentian', pp. 188-196 (9.2 Phonemic Inventory pp. 189-191; 9.3 Phonological Changes pp. 191-195).
sources.note: No statement about Laurentian stress or accent anywhere in ch. 9. The phonemic inventory (p. 189-190) covers consonants and vowels only; p. 190 notes that vowel length 'cannot be determined from the French orthography'. Reconstructed Laurentian forms are written with the Proto-Northern-Iroquoian accent inherited by convention (e.g. La. /ˈahʃẽh/ 'three', /kaˈnõhʃaɁ/ 'house', /ohʃiɁˈtahkõ/ '[on the] foot', /oɁtaˈihẽːh/ 'it is hot', pp. 191-193), i.e. PNI penultimate accent, or antepenultimate when the penult held short *a before a single non-glottal consonant (PNI-6, PNI-7, pp. 120-123). sources.citation: Wikipedia, 'Laurentian language' (accessed 2026-09-17), citing Cartier 1545, Mithun 1999 and Julian 2010.
sources.note: Presumed phoneme inventory only (voiced allophones, nasal vowels, epenthetic vowels); no discussion of stress or accent. Supplied the open MSpace bitstream link for Julian 2010.

sources.citation: Barbeau, Marius. 1961. The language of Canada in the voyages of Jacques Cartier (1534-1538). Contributions to Anthropology 1959 (National Museum of Canada Bulletin 173), 108-229. Newberry Library scan (offprint, 124 pp.).
sources.note: Item-by-item comparison of the ~228 Cartier words with Huron-Wyandot and Six Nations forms recorded by Barbeau himself. The only accent remark is a hand-lettered 'Diacritical marks' key (printed p. 218, p. 112) for Barbeau's own transcriptions of the modern dialects: an acute 'over a vowel shows the main stress or accent. It usually coincides with a rising pitch'; a grave = 'minor or weaker accent'. Nothing on stress in the Cartier/Laurentian forms; his conclusion (pp. 219-221) is that the vocabulary is closest to Huron-Wyandot with 31 items closer to Mohawk.

sources.citation: Biggar, H. P. 1924. The Voyages of Jacques Cartier, published from the originals with translations, notes and appendices. Ottawa: F. A. Acland (Publications of the Public Archives of Canada 11). Vocabularies pp. 80-81 and 241-246; Appendix V (Hale's comparative Wyandot vocabulary) pp. 308 ff.
sources.note: Primary data: the two 16th-c. French-orthography wordlists ('Ensuit le langaige des pays et royaumes de Hochelaga et Canada', p. 241 ff.) with manuscript variants in footnotes. No accent marks in the manuscripts (p. 125 n. 27: 'There are of course no accents of any sort in the MSS'). Hale's appendix gives pronunciation notes for the modern Wyandot comparanda only. No stress information for Laurentian.
